newsitem.title: USA: Analysts see strong U.S. corn, soy plantings.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see strong U.S. corn, soy plantings.

text.p: U.S. farmers, lured by attractive prices, will plant lots of corn and soybeans this year while trimming back on wheat, cotton and rice, analysts said Tuesday.
"Market fundamentals look very good" for corn and soybeans, said USDA chief economist Keith Collins.

In interviews, Collins and two other analysts said they expected about 80 million acres of corn and 64 million acres, or a bit more, or soybeans would be planted this spring -- roughly the same or slightly higher than last year.
In metric measurement, corn acreage would be 31.5 million hectares and soybeans would be 25.2 million hecrates.

Bob Young, co-director of the Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute at the University of Missouri, said plantings would be "probably within spitting distance" of 1996's totals. Corn and soybeans together may rise by one million acres, or 393,701 hectares, he said.

"We expect to see a significant amount of corn planted as well as soybeans," said Mike Hoover of analysts WEFA Group in suburban Philadelphia. "That should add some downward pressure on prices this fall."

The first indication of farmers' plans came last week when the Agriculture Department reported 48.2 million acres (20 million hectares) of winter wheat had been sown for this year's harvest. It was the smallest figure since 1978 and three million acres, or seven percent, less than one year ago.
Half of the winter wheat decline was in seven Midwestern states where corn and soybeans are dominant crops.

"You can make a lot more growing corn and soybeans," said private analyst William Lesher, who noted the new "Freedom to Farm" law removed most limits on what farmers plant. "You look at corn and soybean prices, they're still in good shape."
Wheat prices, while still comparatively high, have fallen from last spring's dizzying levels.
"We would expect the annual kinds of substitutions like a little less rice, a little less cotton (and) a little less wheat," Collins said.

Smaller winter wheat plantings suggested an overall drop in U.S. wheat sowings. Last year's 75.6 million wheat acres (29.8 million hectares) included 52 millon acres (20.5 million hectares) of winter wheat.

Wheat sowings this year may total 72 million acres (28.3 million hectares), Young said. Analysts said spring and durum wheat plantings were likely in the range of 21 million-22 million acres (8.28 million-8.66 million hectares).

Cotton plantings, at 14.7 million acres (5.8 million hectares) in 1996, were too large to be sustained, he said. The 1996 crop was the second largest ever at 18.95 million bales and the second big crop in three years. Cotton merchant William Donavant Jr., at a conference last week, pegged this year's plantings at 13.8 million acres (5.4 million hectares).
Some 2.8 million acres (1.1 million hectares) of rice were planted last year. Young said the "Freedom to Farm" crop-subsidy reform law could result in farmers dropping unprofitable rice land.
